title: The night sky
hookLine: the stars you can see are only the nearest few

cards: Step out of a lit kitchen into a dark yard and, at first, there's almost nothing up there. A few bright points. Maybe a plane.
Give it a few minutes. Your eyes adjust, and more stars come out, faint ones between the bright ones, until the sky that looked empty looks crowded.
Yet every one of those stars, even on the darkest night, is close by, as stars go. Neighbors. The ones you can see with your own eyes are only the nearest few.

teach.h: THE NEAREST PART OF OUR GALAXY.
teach.b: First, the size of what you're seeing. Astronomers say the stars visible to the naked eye all belong to our own galaxy, and to a small nearby part of it.
Beyond them lie stars too faint to see, and beyond those, other galaxies. The night sky you can see is the front porch of something far larger. Second, the light.
Starlight takes time to cross space, so each point is light that left its star long before tonight. You're looking at the past, from many different moments at once.
Third, two old texts that looked up and heard different things. In the book of Job, the voice from the whirlwind turns the stars into questions Job can't answer.
In the King James words: "Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" The stars become a lesson in what Job cannot do.

A psalm looks up at the same sky and asks its own question: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?"

teach.h: THE SKY FILLS IN AS YOU STAY.
teach.b: And the psalm answers that this small creature is crowned with glory and honor. Humbled, and held. Both reactions are honest, and both start with someone standing still long enough to feel their size.
Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a fact.

teach.h: WHAT IS MAN, THAT THOU ART MINDFUL OF HIM?
teach.b: You can read that the visible stars are only the nearest. It lands differently in a dark yard, neck tipped back, as the sky keeps filling in the longer you stay.

how: People who practice stargazing as a practice of awe find a dark place away from lights, let their eyes adjust for several minutes, and look up without hurrying; some read Psalm 8, Job 38 or another text under the sky.

o: a far-off galaxy seen only through the largest telescopes
the hunter's belt of three stars named alongside it in Job
a star cluster named in Job, among stars that are near neighbors

games.q: the night sky — tap the pairs.
p: a nearby part of our galaxy
what is man, that thou art mindful?

s: on a clear night you can see stars in other galaxies
the stars visible to the naked eye all belong to a nearby part of our own galaxy.
the longer you look into a dark sky, the more stars appear

games.q: you're the psalmist. you look up at the moon and the stars and feel very small. where does your song go next?
o: a question, and then: crowned with glory and honor.
silence: there's nothing more to say.
games.why: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" — and the psalm answers that this small creature is crowned with glory and honor.

practice: If it's dark, go to a window or door, turn off the lights behind you and look up; if it's daytime, close your eyes and bring back the darkest night sky you've seen.
Don't look for anything in particular; let the sky fill in, one more faint star with each breath. If you pray, you can let the psalm's question be part of your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Pleiades. One of the star clusters named in the book of Job, a reminder that every star you can see is a near neighbor, light from the past. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the nearest stars. Humbled, and held, under one and the same sky. Until tomorrow.
